what_it_does: Running a large language model on a GPU is expensive partly because GPUs are built for fast parallel math, but LLM token generation is actually bottlenecked by memory speed, not raw compute — leaving most of a GPU's compute capacity sitting idle. CENT replaces the GPU entirely with a cluster of 32 specialized memory modules that do arithmetic right next to where data is stored (called processing-in-memory), connected by CXL — a fast industry-standard link for attaching extra memory to a server — achieving 2.3x higher throughput at 2.9x lower energy and 5.2x more tokens per dollar.
method_in_detail:
The idea. During token generation, a language model's main task is multiplying a single vector (the current token's representation) by enormous weight matrices — one for every layer. This matrix-vector multiply (GEMV) reads a huge amount of data but does very little arithmetic per byte read. GPUs are designed for the opposite: lots of arithmetic per byte. On a 70-billion-parameter model, GPUs sit at only 21% compute utilization. CENT bets that doing the math inside the memory chips — where the bandwidth is 8–16x higher — is a better fit.

The architecture. Each CENT unit is a CXL device (a self-contained module that plugs into a server's memory bus). A CXL switch connects 32 such devices to a host CPU. Inside each device: 16 memory chips, each with two GDDR6-PIM (graphics memory with built-in processing) channels. Each channel has 16 near-bank processing units — small multiply-accumulate engines sitting right next to each bank of memory cells, operating at 32 GFLOPS per channel. This is the PIM (processing in memory) layer. Above it, each device also has PNM (processing near memory) units: 32 exponent accelerators (using a 10-term Taylor series to compute e^x for the softmax step), 32 reduction trees for summing, and 8 small RISC-V processor cores for miscellaneous operations like square root and division. MAC operations (multiply-accumulate, the arithmetic backbone of matrix multiplies) account for over 99% of all arithmetic, so the domain-specific near-bank units handle almost everything.

The key design choice. CXL 3.0's standard protocol has no broadcast primitive (sending one message to many receivers at once), which TP (tensor parallelism — splitting each layer's computation across all 32 devices) requires. CENT adds broadcast by repurposing a reserved field in the CXL packet header to signal the switch to replicate the packet to multiple destinations, enabling collective operations without custom network hardware.

Parallelism. Two strategies: Pipeline Parallel (PP) assigns each transformer block to one device and pipelines multiple user requests through them. Tensor Parallel (TP) splits every weight matrix across all 32 devices, processes a single request faster, and gathers results via broadcast/gather. Hybrid combinations tune the latency-throughput tradeoff.

The result. Compared to 4 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs at similar average power, CENT achieves 2.3x higher throughput, 2.9x lower energy, and 5.2x more tokens per dollar on Llama2-7B/13B/70B. The advantage grows with longer context windows because attention becomes even more memory-bound at scale.
